introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 3 (0750), Paper 3, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer ALL the THREE QUESTIONS. Question ONE carries thirty-four marks and the rest carry thirty-three marks each.

In answering questions on this paper, you are encouraged to refer to your own field and practical work where relevant. Credit will be awarded for such references.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Calculators are allowed. Materials required: Topographic map, Photos, Graph Paper and outline map (where relevant).

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) i) Draw a diagram to show the River Mezam and its tributaries in the area east of easting 03, west of easting 08, north of northing 07 and south of northing 10. Rank the streams using Strahler's method. **(5 marks)**

ii) Calculate the mean bifurcation ratio of River Mezam and its tributaries in the network sketched out in a(i) above and state the significance of your result or answer. **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**What the examiner wants.** (i) A neat sketch of the stream network of ONE block of the map, with every stream given its Strahler order. (ii) A calculation of the bifurcation ratios from your own stream counts, then a meaning for the number. The counts must come from YOUR sketch, so no single set of numbers is the only right answer; the method below is what earns the marks.

**(i) Step 1 - Fix the block.** East of easting 03 and west of easting 08 gives a width of 5 grid squares (5 km); north of northing 07 and south of northing 10 gives a height of 3 grid squares (3 km). At 1:50 000 one grid square is 2 cm, so the block measures 10 cm by 6 cm on the map. In this block the River Mezam crosses the northern part from the west towards the east and south-east, receiving small tributaries from the north and from the south (the labelled river and its blue tributary streams can be seen north of the built-up area).

**Step 2 - Draw.** Draw a rectangle 10 cm by 6 cm (the same scale as the map). Mark the grid lines 03 to 08 and 07 to 10 on the frame. Trace the River Mezam as the thickest line, then each tributary with a thinner line, copying their junctions faithfully. Do not trace contours or roads. Add a title, a north arrow, a scale (1:50 000) and a key.

**Step 3 - Rank by Strahler's method.**
- Order 1: every headstream with no tributary.
- Order 2: formed where TWO order-1 streams meet; order 3: where two order-2 streams meet, and so on.
- When a stream of lower order joins a stream of higher order, the higher order does not change.
Write the order on each segment (1, 2, 3). Then count the streams of each order: N1, N2, N3.

![fig-4](gce-al-geography-2024-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4 is a model of how the finished diagram should look: an ILLUSTRATIVE network (11 first-order, 3 second-order and 1 third-order stream), not the real number read from the map.*

**Marking idea (5 marks).** Frame, scale and north (1); River Mezam and tributaries drawn with correct junctions (2); correct stream orders written on the diagram (2).

**(ii) Bifurcation ratio.** The bifurcation ratio between two successive orders is

Rb = N(u) / N(u+1)

where N(u) is the number of streams of order u. The MEAN bifurcation ratio is the average of all the ratios of the network.

**Worked example (using the model network in figure 4 - replace by your own counts).**

| Order | Number of streams | Ratio |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11 | 11 / 3 = 3.67 |
| 2 | 3 | 3 / 1 = 3.00 |
| 3 | 1 | - |

Mean Rb = (3.67 + 3.00) / 2 = 3.33 (about 3.3).

**Significance.**
- Values of about 3 to 5 are typical of drainage basins in which geology (rock structure) has little distorting effect: the network is well developed and the basin is fairly regular in shape. A mean of about 3.3 therefore suggests a normal, evenly branched network.
- A LOW ratio (near 2) suggests a rounded basin in which tributaries of similar size reach the main river close together, so floodwater arrives together and the flood peak is high and sharp: a flood risk for the town downstream.
- A HIGH ratio (above 5) suggests an elongated or structurally controlled basin, with few large streams and many small ones; the flood peak is lower and flatter.
- For Bamenda, the ratio helps planners judge how quickly rain on the hills becomes a flood in the Mezam valley.

**Mark idea (4 marks).** Formula (1); correct counts and ratios (1 to 2); mean ratio with the right method (1); interpretation (1 to 2).

questions.enonce_markdown: b) Describe and account for the distribution of the road network east of easting 04 and south of northing 09. **(4 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Description (about 2 marks).**
- The roads are very dense and form a close, irregular network, with a small grid of streets, in the built-up centre of Bamenda (roughly eastings 05 to 07, northings 05 to 08).
- Several main roads radiate from this centre: one runs to the north-east and east, another to the south (towards Akum), and others to the west; secondary roads and earth roads branch from them.
- Away from the town, in the south-east part of the block, roads are few: a loop of one road and a few tracks and earth roads, with large areas empty of roads.

**Account (about 2 marks).**
- The town is the administrative, commercial and service centre, so many routes were built to link the people, workplaces and markets: a high density of settlement needs a high density of roads.
- Roads focus on Bamenda because it is a route centre (nodal point) linking neighbouring towns and villages.
- Relief: in the south-east the contour lines are very close together (steep escarpment slopes) and there are rocky areas, so road building is difficult and costly, and few people live there; roads follow the gentler slopes and valleys.
- Low population and few economic activities in the south-east give little reason to build roads.

**Tip.** Point to evidence from the map (grid squares, symbols, contour spacing) in every statement; do not write about Bamenda in general.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) With map evidence only, state:

i) Three functions of Bamenda Town **(3 marks)**

ii) Three reasons why the south east of the map area has scanty settlements **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Functions of Bamenda (any three, 1 mark each, each backed by map evidence).**
- *Administrative function:* the key and map show offices of government (symbols for council, divisional and subdivisional offices, government buildings and the Governor's office label) in and around the town.
- *Residential function:* a large area of urban settlement (the shaded urban symbol) with dense building.
- *Educational function:* symbols of primary and secondary schools and of higher education.
- *Health function:* symbols of hospitals and health centres (for example a divisional hospital is labelled on the map).
- *Religious function:* church and mosque symbols.
- *Transport / route function:* many roads converge on the town from Bafut, Bambui, Akum, Mamfe and the west.
- *Commercial / service function:* a dense street grid and many buildings in the centre, a post office and council offices typical of a town centre.

**(ii) Reasons for scanty settlement in the south-east (any three, 1 mark each).**
- *Steep relief:* contour lines are very close together (an escarpment with steep slopes), so building and farming are difficult.
- *Rocky ground:* the 'rock' symbol covers large areas, with thin soil that cannot support farming or foundations.
- *Poor accessibility:* few roads and only tracks; the area is far from the town and the main road network.
- *Land cover:* shrub/steppe vegetation and scattered farmland suggest poor agricultural land that attracts few farmers.
- *High altitude and exposure* (cooler, windy, little water supply on slopes).

questions.enonce_markdown:
d) i) Using the roads from the west of Bamenda, Bambui, Akum, Mamfe and Bafut, sketch a diagram to show how the roads converge on Bamenda. **(4 marks)**

ii) Identify the type of transport network depicted by your diagram in d (i) above, and state its main advantage. **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Sketch.** Draw a central point or square for Bamenda. From it draw five straight lines (roads) fanning outwards, each ending in a small circle labelled with the place it leads to: Bafut (north-west), Mamfe (west-south-west), Akum (south), Bambui (as read at the east/north-east edge of the map), and the road from the west of Bamenda. Add a title and a short key (road, town, settlement); the directions should match the labels printed at the edge of the map.

![fig-5](gce-al-geography-2024-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

**Marking idea (4 marks).** Central town correctly placed (1); five roads converging (1 to 2); correct labelling and rough directions (1); title, key and neatness (1).

**(ii) Type and advantage.** The network is a **radial (star-shaped, nodal) network**: all roads meet at one central town. Main advantage: every settlement served by a spoke has direct access to Bamenda, so the town is easily reached, which concentrates trade, administration and services and helps it to function as the regional centre (it also makes the exchange of goods and people between the surrounding villages and the town fast and cheap).

questions.enonce_markdown: e) Using map evidence, state TWO likely causes of water scarcity in Bamenda Town? **(2 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two, 1 mark each, with map evidence:
- *High demand from a large, dense population:* the shaded urban area is large and densely built, so the number of users outgrows the supply from the few streams.
- *Few permanent streams in the built-up core:* the main river and its tributaries lie mostly along the northern margin of the town; the centre and the southern and eastern districts are far from a stream, and some streams are only temporary or seasonal, so supply falls in the dry season.
- *Sloping, built-up ground:* steep slopes and hard surfaces (roofs, roads) increase run-off and reduce infiltration, so little water is stored in the soil and springs; the town is also on high ground above the streams, so water must be pumped up.
- *Pollution of the streams* running through or beside the built-up area (wastes from settlements), which makes the water unfit to use.

questions.enonce_markdown:
f) Study the photograph below which shows a geographical phenomena and answer the questions which follow:

![fig-3](gce-al-geography-2024-p3-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Photo for question 1 (f).*

i) Identify and describe the problem shown on the photograph. **(2 marks)**

ii) State Two possible causes of the problem identified in (f)i) **(2 marks)**

iii) Suggest three measures that can be adopted to solve the problem identified in (f) i) above. **(3 marks)**
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) The problem: flooding.** The photograph is an aerial view of a built-up area inundated by brown, silt-laden water. A wide river flows beside the settlement; its water has overflowed its banks and spread over streets, gardens and open land, so that houses stand surrounded or partly covered by water and only the roofs and tree tops show. (Naming and describing: 1 mark; description with evidence: 1 mark.)

**(ii) Two possible causes (1 mark each).**
- Very heavy or prolonged rainfall filling the river beyond the capacity of its channel (overbank flow).
- Houses built on the flood plain next to the river, with poor or blocked drainage and hard surfaces that increase run-off.
- (Also acceptable: deforestation of the upper catchment, siltation of the channel, failure or opening of a dam, climate change.)

**(iii) Three measures (1 mark each).**
- Build and maintain drainage channels, culverts and embankments (levees), and dredge the river to raise its capacity.
- Zone the land: forbid building on flood plains, and relocate the people at risk to higher ground.
- Plant trees and keep vegetation in the catchment to slow run-off; protect wetlands.
- Set up flood forecasting and early-warning systems and prepare emergency plans.
- Regulate river flow by dams and reservoirs (storage).
